card.thesis: This engine cannot express relative strength -- entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest sector' or trade a spread. What this card does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, a confirmed non-extreme uptrend -- identically across 12 names, one per GICS sector (two in Consumer Discretionary, for reasons given below), and cap concurrent holdings at 4 of 12. That cap plus the universe's fill order is the only 'rotation' logic available. The prior semis rotation card (A-rotation) ran this exact entry/exit/stop/target/hold-day logic against 9 correlated chip names (mean pairwise correlation 0.589) and called the result a concentrated sector bet, not a rotation. This card changes exactly one variable -- the universe's correlation structure -- to test whether breadth itself is worth anything: XOM (Energy), CAT (Industrials), HD and MCD (Consumer Discretionary, housing vs. restaurant spend), KO (Staples), JNJ (Health Care), JPM (Financials), MSFT (Info Tech, no fab exposure), VZ (Communication Services), NEE (Utilities), LIN (Materials), PLD (Real Estate). Measured trailing-253-session pairwise correlation through 2026-02-13: mean 0.245, versus 0.589 for the incumbent semis book -- roughly 2.4x more diversified by this measure. Universe order is not alphabetical: names are ordered by ascending average correlation to the rest of the book (MSFT 0.12 lowest, LIN 0.36 highest), so when more than 4 names qualify on the same session -- which happens on about 71% of sessions in the trailing two years -- the broker's fixed fill order fills the most-diversifying names first, the one ordering rule available that is actually about breadth rather than an arbitrary tiebreak. Selection is not index-derived: these names were chosen and ordered by measured correlation structure and liquidity, not by picking 'the largest member of each sector' off today's constituent list, so the card is not subject to the universe_knowable_from gate on that basis -- though every name here is, in fact, a company that survived to be listed today, and that is a real limit on what this backtest can show, stated plainly rather than hidden. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders across multiple unrelated sectors who already positioned before this rule confirms; mean-reversion sellers fading strength inside a still-intact uptrend in any one of these sectors; and the fact that a rule this permissive, when it fires on names in 8+ different sectors at once, describes 'the market is going up,' not a sector call -- in which case this basket simply behaves like a slow, capped SPY substitute, and diversification purchased no edge, only lower variance.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 55 and rsi(14) < 80

card.display_name: C15 - Volatility Shock Reversal: leveraged financials & cyclicals
card.thesis: Mechanism: a single-name true-range day at least 1.5x its own ATR(14), closing down (close<open) and already oversold (rsi(14)<30), is a volatility shock -- forced or reflexive selling that has temporarily overwhelmed the name's normal liquidity, not (in most cases) a full repricing of fair value in one session. The counterparty on the other side of my entry is whoever sold into that shock day at the worst print of the move: margin-called leveraged longs, risk-parity/vol-targeting funds cutting gross exposure mechanically as realized vol jumps, and short-covering-driven air pockets on the way down. None of those sellers are pricing the business; they are meeting a risk constraint. I am buying from them at the next session's open (the broker's fill convention) and selling into the reflex bounce, via crosses_above sma(10), a short stop, or a 10-day time cap if neither arrives. This is a short-horizon, volatility-triggered reversal, not a fundamental dip-buy -- the entry gate is defined entirely by the magnitude of the move (ATR multiple) rather than by trend context, which is what makes it a volatility-discipline card rather than a mean-reversion one built on RSI level alone. Falsification: if the shock is not noise but new, correctly-priced information -- a name is genuinely insolvent, guidance is permanently impaired, a business model is broken -- the 'bounce' will not arrive before the stop or the time cap, and the strategy just bought a falling knife repeatedly. That is precisely what I expect happens in gfc: several of these financials (C, BAC, AIG, MS, GS, WFC) had genuinely impaired balance sheets in 2008, not merely a liquidity air-pocket, so the reversal mechanism should fail hardest exactly there, which is why I name gfc as my predicted worst window rather than treating the mechanism as universal. Selection and index status: this universe is NOT index-derived. I did not draw it from data/universe/index-constituents.json and I am not relying on any 'these are today's S&P 500 members' fact. I chose money-center banks, a broker-dealer pair, an insurer, an auto manufacturer and a miner because balance-sheet leverage and operating/commodity cyclicality are structural, multi-decade properties of these business types (a levered bank's equity is a leveraged claim on assets, so its volatility is structurally higher than an unlevered industrial's, in any decade) and because I required, before looking at any trading-window return, (a) price history to at least 2000 so the card can be judged in gfc, covid, q4-2018 and both chop windows, and (b) trailing-year ATR/price ratios through 2026-02-13 clustered tightly enough that one stop-loss and one position size are a defensible approximation across the whole book (see measurements below) -- the same non-window-scanning selection discipline the prior round's G-volatility card used, applied here to a sector nobody else in this round's field has touched (every other card I found in data/rounds/r3-2026-08/cards -- B-wide, C-wide, c12, c13, c14, c16, c17 -- is built on AI/semis/cloud names, staples/utilities, or a Treasury/gold flight-to-quality basket). I explicitly did not use my knowledge of which of these names crashed hardest in 2008 to choose among them -- the shortlist I scored (C, BAC, MS, GS, AIG, WFC, F, FCX, OXY, SLB, JPM, COF, BIIB, REGN, MRVL) is a structural sector list scored on ATR/price and history length alone, and the 10 finalists are simply the subset with the tightest dispersion cluster, not the subset with the biggest 2008 drawdown.
card.entry: high - low > atr(14) * 1.5 and close < open and rsi(14) < 30

card.thesis: Institutional flow into AI/cloud-infrastructure leaders re-rates them in slow, multi-week waves, not single days: a fund building a position over weeks pushes the medium-term average through the long-term one, and that crossover is a public, mechanical signal other trend-following capital reacts to next, extending the move further than any one participant intended. On the design-window history of these 12 names, once close > sma(200) is already established and ema(20) crosses above ema(50) -- a fresh acceleration inside a standing uptrend, not a bottom-pick -- the resulting move has a median duration of roughly 3-4 weeks and stretches past two months at the 75th percentile (NVDA's longest such run reached 256 sessions, MSFT's 169, TSM's 189). The other side of this trade is whoever sells into that strength: value-discipline holders trimming into a re-rate, and short sellers pressing a name that 'already ran too far' -- both wrong, on average, while the wave is still building. I tested a fixed take-profit and a fast rule exit against simply riding the position to a stop or a genuine trend break, on this same entry: capping gains at 8-30% cut mean per-signal return to 2-9%, and a fast 20-day-EMA exit (even with a 3-day confirmation filter) cut it to 3-5% and win rate to 42-49% by whipsawing out of live trends on ordinary pullbacks. Letting the position run to a stop, a 200-day trend-break, or a 180-day backstop produced roughly triple the aggregate return of either capped variant, at the cost of a median trade near breakeven-to-slightly-negative -- this strategy's edge is concentrated in a minority of large winners, which is exactly what a take-profit would have amputated. It is deliberately not diversified across volatility regimes: the universe was chosen so one stop and one position size fit all 12 names reasonably rather than being tuned to any single one.
card.entry: ema(20) crosses_above ema(50) and close > sma(200)

card.display_name: B-wide - B-momentum rules, mechanically chosen universe
card.thesis: This card exists to attribute a difference, not to win. It is Strategy B's rules -- the same ema(20)/ema(50) cross inside a close>sma(200) regime, the same 12% stop, the same 180-day cap, the same 6 slots at 15% -- pointed at a universe chosen by a rule instead of by an analyst. B-momentum's twelve names are a hand-picked AI and cloud-infrastructure book; this card's twelve are simply the most heavily traded index constituents with history back to 2004, ranked by median dollar volume over the design year and frozen. The two books overlap on the semiconductor complex and diverge everywhere else -- this one carries UNH, LLY and MSTR, which no thematic AI screen would have produced. If the wider store is worth having, a mechanical draw from it should not be far behind a curated one; if the curation was the whole edge, this card should underperform B materially and that is the finding. Note what this does and does not isolate: a twelve-name universe cannot be 'widened', only swapped, so this changes the universe and the selection method together. It does not claim to isolate breadth alone.
card.entry: ema(20) crosses_above ema(50) and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: AI-capex-cycle names re-rate on multi-quarter earnings-revision cycles, not single days: a data-center or cloud demand cycle shows up as a sequence of beat-and-raise quarters that institutional allocators scale into over months, not one print. That flow creates serial correlation in price that a same-day oscillator cannot see. The other side of the trade is investors who sell into strength too early, anchored to a pre-cycle 'fair value', and investors who panic-sell the first pullback inside an intact uptrend, mistaking noise for reversal -- both hand the rest of the move to a slower, rule-following holder. I measured this rather than assuming it: on this universe's last ~1500 sessions (~6y) through 2026-02-13, a close>sma(200) regime filter plus a 20/50-EMA crossover trigger produced 77 trades at 49.4% win rate, but average winners (+29.6%) were 4.1x average losers (-7.3%), and winning trades were held a median of 118 days vs 16 for losers -- the classic trend signature of a system that is right less than half the time and still profitable because it cuts losses fast and lets the rest run. The chop problem is real and I confronted it directly: the same golden-cross setup on this universe's smaller, more speculative names (IREN, OKLO, APLD, BE, KORU) produced negative average 60-day forward returns after the signal fired -- those names were excluded from the universe below specifically because the measured data showed the entries do not sustain here, not because of a prior. Within the chosen universe, widening the stop from 8% to 12% cut stop-outs from 12/77 (16%) to 7/77 (9%) while barely moving mean trade return (0.093->0.093), meaning most of the discarded stop-outs at the tighter level were noise, not real breakdowns -- direct evidence the wider stop survives chop without giving back the move. The regime filter (sma200) plus a medium-term trigger (ema20/50, not raw ema50/200) was chosen over a textbook dual-moving-average cross because it produces materially fewer whipsaw entries on this universe's large, liquid AI/semi/software names, at the cost of entering somewhat later into each trend.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.display_name: C-wide - C-trend rules, mechanically chosen universe
card.thesis: The same experiment as B-wide, on the slower book. C-trend's rules are unchanged -- close>sma(200) as the regime filter, ema(20)/ema(50) as the trigger, ema(20) crossing back below ema(50) as the exit, 12% stop, 120-day cap, 5 slots at 18% -- and only the nine names change, from a hand-picked AI/semi list to the nine most heavily traded long-history index constituents by median dollar volume through the design cutoff. C-trend's own memo argues its edge comes from excluding speculative names whose golden crosses do not sustain; a liquidity screen is a different and much blunter way of excluding them, and this card measures what that costs. As with B-wide, a nine-name universe is swapped rather than widened, so universe and selection rule move together.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.display_name: Blue-Chip RSI Reversion — Wide Sector Book
card.thesis: Mechanism: a 14-day RSI reading below 30 in a mature, high-float, heavily-owned single stock that is still trading above its 150-day SMA is short-horizon, largely non-fundamental selling pressure inside an intact intermediate trend -- single-name news overreaction (a guidance miss, a downgrade, a lawsuit headline), index-fund and closet-indexer rebalancing flow that is price-insensitive by construction, and short-term momentum/CTA selling that fades once the news cycle clears. These are mature large-caps with active buyback programs and broad analyst coverage, which put a latent, valuation-aware bid under the stock once the panic-driven flow is done -- buyback desks, value-tilted funds and short-term dip buyers are the counterparty I am trading against, buying from forced or reflexive sellers who are not pricing the business, and selling to them (via the RSI>55 exit) once sentiment normalizes but before the move can be mistaken for a fresh trend leg. The 150-day trend filter is the same 'nothing structural has changed yet' proxy used elsewhere in this round, just faster than a 200-day filter because single stocks re-rate faster than diversified ETFs. Pre-registered failure regime: a fast, deep, systemic decline where 150-day SMAs across the whole book have not yet turned down before the crash accelerates (COVID's Feb-Mar 2020 leg is the clearest historical case in my own sample; GFC's Sep-Oct 2008 leg is the plausible second case, though I have only one qualifying signal in that exact window). In that regime the entry keeps firing on 'dips' that are actually the first third of a systemic decline correlated across every name in the book at once -- the diversification this book is built on works against single-stock idiosyncratic risk but does nothing against a market-wide air pocket -- so the RSI>55 exit does not arrive inside the 15-day hold, several positions hit the 7% stop simultaneously, and losses cluster in the same handful of sessions rather than being spread out.

A confirmed swing-high breakout is the point at which the resting supply that had capped a stock at its last significant pivot has been absorbed; the marginal buyer transacting above that level does so with less overhead resistance than existed a session earlier, and the marginal seller who anchored to the old high as fair value is now underwater and stepping aside rather than defending a broken level. The 200-day trend filter restricts entries to names whose broader supply/demand balance already favors buyers, so a breakout is read as continuation of an existing imbalance rather than a reversal bet on a name that has been going nowhere. The counterparty on the other side of a fill is not a rational price-setter reacting to the breakout itself: it is a momentum-agnostic seller (an index-fund rebalancer, a tax-loss seller, an investor rotating out of the name for reasons unrelated to its chart) or a trend-following short who is stopped out as the level gives way. Neither is pricing the breakout; that mispricing is the edge being harvested, and it should decay if enough capital chases the same signal. This card spreads that one mechanism across six economically distinct sectors -- semiconductors, e-commerce/big-box retail, heavy industrial equipment, energy services, money-center banking, and managed care/pharma -- specifically so a result speaks to the mechanism rather than to one sector's beta, which a single-sector or single-asset-class breakout card cannot separate.
card.entry: close crosses_above swing_high(20) and close > sma(200)

card.display_name: C14 - Risk-managed: flight-to-quality basket, built for the worst window
card.thesis: This card is not trying to top the median-return table. It is designed for the worst-window column of the Pareto frontier: when equities are in genuine distress, capital does not evaporate, it moves -- into long and intermediate Treasuries, into gold, and to a lesser extent into investment-grade credit -- because those are the instruments large pools of capital are mandated or incentivised to hold when risk appetite collapses (pension and insurance duration-matching flows, safe-haven gold demand, and credit's senior claim relative to equity). The other side of every one of my trades is whoever is still selling those instruments into the flight, or the momentum/carry trader whose short-duration or short-vol position gets forced out; I am not claiming an edge over them in normal markets, only that I am positioned to be a buyer of what they are forced to sell exactly when SPY is worst. I measured this rather than assumed it, using only data through 2026-02-13. Buy-and-hold cumulative return of my four names, TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD, against SPY over every window fully inside the design cutoff: gfc (Oct07-Mar09) TLT +25.1% IEF +20.2% GLD +23.9% LQD -6.8% vs SPY -55.2%; covid (Feb-Jun20) TLT +13.3% IEF +7.9% GLD +10.3% LQD +3.7% vs SPY -7.9%; q4-2018 TLT +4.6% IEF +3.3% GLD +5.8% LQD -1.1% vs SPY -19.3%; chop-2011 TLT +34.3% IEF +14.5% GLD +6.1% LQD +9.0% vs SPY +1.3%. Every one of those four is a case where equities were flat-to-crushed and this basket was flat-to-strongly-positive. But I also measured the counter-case rather than hide it: bear-2022 TLT -29.3% IEF -15.4% GLD -7.3% LQD -21.1% vs SPY -24.5% -- when the shock is rate hikes rather than a growth/credit scare, duration is not a hedge, it is a second source of loss, and my basket did no better than equities and TLT individually did worse. I also checked equity 'defensive sector' alternatives (XLU, XLP) before excluding them: both fell 28-42% during gfc and 11-21% during covid, worse than SPY's own covid drawdown in XLU's case -- they are equities first and defensive second, and a credit-crisis or liquidity-crisis regime takes them down with everything else, so they do not belong in a card whose whole claim is about crisis behaviour. I also checked SLV as a second precious-metal sleeve and excluded it: -22% in chop-2011, -17% in bear-2022, -5% in gfc -- an inconsistent diversifier that would have added a name without adding ballast on the exact days that matter.
card.entry: close > sma(150) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30) and rsi(14) < 70

card.thesis: C-trend's mechanism -- a close>sma(200) regime filter plus an ema(20)/ema(50) crossover trigger -- is measured on AI-capex-cycle names whose multi-quarter earnings-revision cascades are the stated source of the serial correlation it exploits. This card asks whether the same mechanical rule captures any edge on twelve large-cap names picked from staples, healthcare, utilities, industrials, energy and financials -- sectors whose trends are not driven by earnings-revision cascades but by slower macro cycles: rate-sensitive rotation into/out of utilities and REIT-adjacent industrials, defensive-vs-cyclical rotation around growth scares, and multi-year commodity or credit cycles for energy and financials. The other side of this trade is the same in kind as C-trend's, different in speed: momentum and growth allocators who ignore 'boring' dividend payers during risk-on stretches, ceding the slow continuation to whoever is still holding when the rotation turns, plus value investors who sell a defensive name the moment it looks 'expensive' relative to its own history and miss the back half of a multi-quarter re-rating. I measured this rather than assumed it (detail in point 3): the entry fires plausibly across every name (28-47 signals per symbol over 22 years, comparable per-symbol frequency to C-trend's), but the edge it captures is real and measurably weaker than the AI-complex version -- a finding the brief asked this card to surface honestly rather than paper over with a flattering universe.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)
